stories.topic: The Bionic Man and His Airport Problem
stories.summary: Amit teases Ajay open the show by drawing the great existential difference between them: Amit is a flesh-and-blood organic human, Ajay is a 'bionic man.' Ajay has had a metal rod in his leg since age 19 (after a crash) and has recently added a titanium implant in his jaw. The downside: he sets off airport security every time, which is why he has switched to half-sleeve shirts.
stories.insight: The lightest possible setup for a serious episode about machinery and humans: even a deeply analytical economist's body is a make-versus-buy story. The body wears down; we contract out replacement parts and adapt our wardrobe to live with them.

stories.summary: In 1958 Nehru's India produced a document called the Science Policy Resolution, articulating the dream of building the country on rationalism, looking beyond superstition, and harnessing science as 'a way of life, an approach to the world, and an instrument path to making the country better.' Ajay calls it 'goosebump material' and includes long extracts in his paper. IIT Bombay was founded the same year — the dates rhyme.
stories.insight: The post-independence project of Indian science was dreamy and stirring even when its execution methods (build government labs with civil-servant scientists) were imperfect. Honour the dream; rethink the methods. The right test of a 1958 idea today is not whether the dream is wrong but whether 1947's only-feasible implementation is still the only one available.

stories.topic: TIFR and BARC Began as Tata Projects
stories.summary: Many Indians don't realise that two of India's flagship scientific institutions — TIFR and BARC — actually began as private initiatives of the Tata group, then were handed over to the Union government after independence. Once absorbed, they became government-funded organisations with civil servant scientists, and became the template for everything that followed: ICMR, ICAR, DRDO, CSIR, ISRO and others, all 'make' rather than 'buy.'
stories.insight: What looks today like inevitable state-led science was a contingent post-independence choice. The most iconic 'public' science institutions in India were originally private — a useful corrective for anyone who assumes innovation must originate in the state.

stories.topic: The Israeli Blabbermouths vs. Apple's Sealed Lips
stories.summary: Two extreme cultures of knowledge spillover. Apple in Silicon Valley is a low-spillover environment: NDAs are aggressively enforced, employees keep their mouths shut, and outsiders cannot guess the next product. Israel is the opposite — every scientist and engineer has gone through army conscription with comrades from other firms; informal trust networks transcend corporate boundaries; knowledge leaks constantly between firms in friendly side conversations. That is precisely why Israel's innovation ecosystem is so productive.
stories.insight: Innovation depends on porosity. The same secrecy that protects a firm's profits drains a society's spillover. Israel's accidental advantage is that the state forced bonds between people across firms before commerce ever began — a non-replicable structural feature that explains far more than 'Israeli grit' ever could.

stories.topic: JPL Has Sat Inside Caltech Since the 1960s
stories.summary: The Jet Propulsion Laboratory — the nerve centre of every NASA interplanetary mission, including the spacecraft flying to Mars and Jupiter — is not a government facility. It sits physically inside Caltech, a private university, as a long-standing NASA contract that has run since the 1960s. Thousands of JPL scientists are physically embedded among Caltech faculty, with constant coffee-table cross-pollination in both directions.
stories.insight: Most people imagine 'contracting out' as the canteen vendor. The real American innovation model contracts out the control room of interplanetary exploration to a private university — and has done so for sixty years. The depth of US contracting capability is the secret sauce of NASA, not its rocket scientists.

stories.topic: NASA Made the Integrated Circuit Industry
stories.summary: Before there was a market for integrated circuits, there was NASA. Spacecraft demanded miniaturisation in a way that earthbound circuit boards never had to bother with, so when the IC arrived NASA was the first and for a while the only buyer. Every early IC firm was running on NASA contracts. The entire modern semiconductor industry — every CPU you use today — is downstream of those early NASA research contracts demanding small, light circuits for spacecraft.
stories.insight: Genuine spillovers from public R&D can be staggering. A space agency commissioning miniature circuits for rockets accidentally seeded the entire civilian computing revolution. The lesson is not that the state always picks winners — it is that demanding, contracted-out research from a credible buyer can pull whole industries into existence.

stories.summary: At the end of WWII, the US and the Soviets raced to capture German rocket scientists. Many of these scientists were die-hard Nazis — too dangerous to be released into American society. The US military dumped them all into an obscure cow town in Alabama called Huntsville, with a new lab and semi-imprisonment. Two generations later, Huntsville has grown into one of the great scientific and engineering R&D capitals of the world — because those people raised families, taught their children, and lifted local schools.
stories.insight: Concentrate scientific talent in a single physical place and the long compounding effect on regional capability is staggering. The seeding of even a small number of remarkable people, given decades and roots, transforms a place. The story is morally awkward (it begins with Nazis) but the human-capital lesson is real and patient.

stories.summary: Amit's father told him that after the British left, while many talented Indians signed up for the Nehruvian project of building the central state, others quietly chose the opposite. They went to one village at a time and dug in — committing their whole lives to one community. Generations later, those villages are visibly different: better hygiene, better education, better status of women. The compounding of one remarkable person stuck to one place is real.
stories.insight: A lovely echo of the Huntsville insight from the opposite political end. Concentration of talent and patience over decades is the formula whether you call it post-Nazi rocket science or Gandhian village uplift. The thing the modern Indian state most lacks is not money but a willingness to play the multi-generation game.

stories.topic: The Limerick On The Mosquitoes Of Versova
stories.summary: When Ajay observes that Indian mosquitoes change every two hundred kilometres, Amit one-ups him: it's actually less. He used to be a professional limerick writer for The Times of India and once wrote a limerick on the mosquitoes of Versova specifically — the Mumbai suburb. He promises to dig it up and put it on screen.
stories.insight: A small, charming detour into hyper-local knowledge: the variation that sits inside the country is finer than any abstract theory captures. It is also the perfect set-up for the show's later case that humanities and social sciences cannot be free-ridden from abroad — the mosquitoes of Versova will not be characterised in Washington.

stories.summary: Confronted with the objection that overhauling Indian science policy will take twenty years, Ajay quotes Larry Summers: 'If a tree will take twenty years to grow, then I want to run outside and plant the sapling right now.' His paper proposes a calm, twenty-year non-disruptive transition for ISRO and a couple of other organisations — not an upheaval, but a journey that begins today.
stories.insight: The objection 'this will take twenty years' is not an argument against starting; it is an argument for starting immediately. The Indian impulse to wait until political conditions are perfect simply pushes the harvest twenty years further out.

recommendations.item: Rethinking innovation policy in India: Amplifying spillovers through contracting-out
recommendations.creator: RA Mashelkar, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas
recommendations.context: The XKDR Forum paper at the heart of this entire episode.
recommendations.reason: Amit insisted Ajay recommend his own paper so he wouldn't cop out. Amit calls it awesome — clear, rigorous, written in plain English unlike most academic papers. It lays out the make-vs-buy decision for state R&D, why contracting out generates spillovers, and a concrete twenty-year transition path for organisations like ISRO.

recommendations.item: How Innovation Works: And Why It Flourishes in Freedom
recommendations.creator: Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Ridley's book on innovation as a bottom-up emergent process.
recommendations.reason: Amit's chosen counter to top-down innovation policy. Ridley argues innovation is a bottom-up process within society, fuelled by freedom and decentralised experimentation — a frame that supports Amit's skepticism about whether the state should be in this business at all.

recommendations.item: Huntsville, Alabama
recommendations.context: An R&D city in Alabama that grew out of relocated German rocket scientists post-WWII.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's 'oddball' recommendation — visit it but more importantly study it. A live demonstration of how concentrating scientific talent in one place compounds, over generations, into a regional engineering powerhouse. The deep lesson about clusters and patience that runs through the episode.

recommendations.item: Why Talent Comes in Clusters (Episode 8, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A bonus recommendation tied to the Huntsville case study.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's bonus pairing for the Huntsville recommendation: their own earlier episode on why talent comes in clusters, the structural argument behind the Huntsville miracle and the Indian villagers who stayed.

recommendations.item: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column laying out his central political-economy claim.
recommendations.reason: Foundational reference for Amit's first point of skepticism. Government action is funded by coerced taxes; every action therefore carries a moral cost. Each ideology is really an argument about when this cost is justified — and innovation policy, on Amit's list, sits low against rule of law and city management.

recommendations.item: Understanding the State (Episode 25, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier foundational episode on the state.
recommendations.reason: Amit invokes it explicitly to ground his skepticism: the state's monopoly on violence, the great liberal paradox of ceding rights to protect rights, and the moral implications of every coerced rupee.

recommendations.item: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their episode on market failure as the trigger for state intervention.
recommendations.reason: The companion to Episode 25, used here to define the technical sense of 'market failure' — externalities (positive and negative) — that underpins the entire case for innovation spending.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier episode on India's economic story.
recommendations.reason: Amit cites it to make the unseen-cost argument: top-down statist policy kept hundreds of millions in poverty for decades longer than necessary. The 'unseen' lost output of those decades is the moral counterweight to the 'seen' triumph of the IIT-fed IT industry.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (Episode 387, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
recommendations.context: A 9-hour-53-minute deep dive on India's economic journey.
recommendations.reason: Amit's recommended deep dive when readers want the long account of the costs of India's post-independence economic policy choices that the innovation-policy debate is layered on top of.

recommendations.item: Biju Rao Won't Bow to Conventional Wisdom (Episode 392, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Biju Rao
recommendations.context: Amit's deep dive with the economist Biju Rao.
recommendations.reason: One of Amit's favourites. Rao's central insight maps onto the episode's argument: you can't govern from a distance. Sitting in Washington reading data is no substitute for hands-dirty fieldwork. Especially relevant to the case for Indian-specific research the world will not do for us.

recommendations.item: India Needs Decentralization (Episode 47, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier episode on the subsidiarity principle.
recommendations.reason: Amit explicitly uses the subsidiarity principle — government action belongs at the lowest viable level — and notes the parallel: the choice between adopting foreign innovation and producing it locally is a kind of subsidiarity for knowledge.

recommendations.item: Mosquitoes As Big As A Bus
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column linked from the show notes, alluding to the local Versova mosquito limerick.
recommendations.reason: The piece behind the line about Versova mosquitoes; an example of hyper-local Indian knowledge that no abroad researcher would ever produce.

recommendations.item: Covid-19 in the tropics: How will high heat and humidity shape the outcomes?
recommendations.creator: Suja Thomas
recommendations.context: Cited as an example of uniquely-Indian COVID research.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's exemplar of work that nobody outside India will do: how COVID transmits in Indian homes, with their cross-ventilation, fans, heat and humidity. The kind of question that demonstrates why a country needs its own research capability even in a free-riding age.

recommendations.item: The industry structure of India's large firms: IT is the biggest industry
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's column documenting that IT and IT-enabled services dominate India's corporate sector.
recommendations.reason: Empirical backing for Ajay's one-line summary of India: IT and IT-enabled services produced for the West. The article is the data behind his claim that early Nehru-era science investment seeded today's largest Indian industry.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Source of two crucial concepts woven through the episode: the marginal cost of public funds (Rs 3 of GDP cost for every Rs 1 of state spending) and the 'invisible infrastructure' framing — the hidden contracting and rule-of-law layers without which grand projects fail.

recommendations.item: Public Finance at XKDR
recommendations.context: Ajay's organisation's public-finance research field.
recommendations.reason: Where the contracting-knowledge-meets-science-policy collaboration with Mashelkar began. The portal links to the body of work behind this paper.

recommendations.item: When Ideas Have Sex
recommendations.creator: Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Ridley's famous TED-style talk on the recombination of ideas as the engine of innovation.
recommendations.reason: Amit invokes the title to make the case that contracting out R&D physically multiplies sites of idea collision — labs, PhD students, private firms — and that this is precisely what generates spillovers. Ridley's frame is the pro-spillover counterpart to Amit's freedom-flourishes argument.

recommendations.item: The Martian
recommendations.creator: Ridley Scott
recommendations.context: Cited via Ajay's quip that India's Mars Orbiter Mission cost less than the movie about going to Mars.
recommendations.reason: A cultural touchstone for the boast about ISRO's frugal Mars mission — and a hint, given the rest of the episode, that frugality of one craft is no substitute for spillovers into society.

recommendations.item: How to Do Development (Episode 57, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode on development practice.
recommendations.reason: Listed among the prior EIE episodes in this loose trilogy of state-and-society debates that this episode builds on.

recommendations.item: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Episode 55, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier episode on Indian infrastructure.
recommendations.reason: Companion episode that fed the same first-principles questioning of the state's role in big visible projects.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 56, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier episode on education policy.
recommendations.reason: Cited alongside the infrastructure episode as a precedent for opening the box and asking first-principles questions about state involvement — the same template applied here to innovation.

recommendations.item: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Episode 56, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE episode skeptical of state-built digital infrastructure.
recommendations.reason: A reference point for Amit's structural worry that Indian state initiatives in technology become extractive or bureaucratic in practice — the same frame he carries into innovation policy.

recommendations.item: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier episode on the knowledge ecosystem.
recommendations.reason: Amit references it while noting that the pipeline question — how academic papers become columns become policy — deserves its own episode rather than being squeezed in here.

core_ideas.concept: Make vs Buy in State R&D
core_ideas.explanation: The central conceptual move of the paper. Every organisation faces a make-versus-buy choice (build it in-house or contract it out), and Indian science policy after 1947 chose 'make' by default — government labs with civil-servant scientists. The paper argues 'buy' is structurally superior for R&D: contract universities and private firms to do the research, fund multiple rival pathways, and accept that some will fail. Knowledge then resides in society, not in a hermetic state tower.
core_ideas.quote: Our objective is not to make the Indian state great. Our objective is to make India great.

core_ideas.explanation: The technical case for state spending on innovation. When a firm or person invests in research, only part of the gain is captured privately — the rest spills over to society as knowledge, talent, patents, reverse-engineerable products, and informal conversations between friends. That wedge means private actors systematically under-invest. The state can correct this by raising tax revenue and spending it specifically in ways that maximise spillovers.
core_ideas.quote: The total gain to society may be 100, but only 40 is captured by [the firm]. So each individual, each firm tends to underinvest in innovative activities.

core_ideas.explanation: From Kelkar and Shah's In Service of the Republic. Every rupee the government raises costs roughly Rs 3 of GDP — through compliance costs, distortions, behavioural avoidance, and the lawyers and accountants needed to administer it. Therefore the state should not spend a rupee unless the social gain is at least three rupees. This is the discipline that prevents 'science is good, let's spend more.' The corollary debated here is whether 3x social gain is by itself sufficient — Amit pushes back that costs and benefits accruing to different people make even a 3x deal morally non-automatic.
core_ideas.quote: To justify a spending of one, you've got to feel that the gains to society are about three.

core_ideas.explanation: Behind every visible state achievement (NASA's missions, NHAI highways) is a layer of unsexy administrative machinery: contracting capability, the rule of law, fraud detection, grant disbursal, founding documents. NASA looks like rocket scientists; what really enables it is hidden chapters of US procurement law and decades of contracting craft. India's invisible infrastructure is partly missing — research scholars wait years for grants, contracts go to cronies — and rebuilding it is a multi-generation project.
core_ideas.quote: When you see the glory of NASA, what people are not appreciating is how chapters inside the GFR equivalent of the United States made all this possible.

core_ideas.explanation: A poor country should be unembarrassedly grateful for the trillions the West pours into R&D and should free-ride on the bulk of it. Transistors, Unix, thermodynamics, mRNA vaccines, COVID Shield — none had to be invented in India. The strategic question is the residual: which problems are genuinely Indian (tropical diseases, drones at 18,000 feet in Ladakh, COVID transmission in cross-ventilated homes, humanities and social sciences) and therefore cannot be free-ridden? That residual is the legitimate domain for Indian state-funded research.
core_ideas.quote: Solar panels now cost less than plastic panels.

core_ideas.concept: Why Research Needs Multiple Rival Pathways
core_ideas.explanation: If there is no possibility of failure, it is not research — it is development. Research, by definition, requires risk and many parallel rival approaches; some will work, some won't, all will create knowledge. Government settings cannot tolerate this: bureaucratic approvals collapse on a single path, internal political economy snuffs out rivals, the CAG cannot understand 'we tried it and it failed.' Contracting out is the only structurally honest way to fund risky research, because the state can stand back, fund six rival vaccine teams, and double down on the two that work.
core_ideas.quote: If there is no possibility of failure, it's not research.

core_ideas.explanation: How to actually do the make-to-buy transition. (1) Amend the General Financial Rules (GFR) to add chapters that recognise grants and cost-plus contracts — instruments alien to the current rulebook. (2) Rewrite each scientific organisation's founding document so that contracting out becomes the default — the way NHAI's founding document mandated contracting rather than direct construction. (3) Build process manuals and the legal-engineering-scientific staff to actually run grants and cost-plus agreements. None of this is glamour work; all of it is necessary.
core_ideas.quote: Our job is not to build a spacecraft, our job is to do contracts.

core_ideas.explanation: A practical insight that simplifies the change problem. There are nominally hundreds of Indian science organisations, but functionally only about five matter — ISRO and a handful of large councils. A change programme that retools just one or two of these existing organisations and creates one or two new ones (an Indian NIH for health-research financing, a DARPA-style risk-taking agency) would deliver most of the gain. No upheaval; a 20-year non-disruptive journey.
core_ideas.quote: Maybe bite off one one, take one old organization, start one new organization.

core_ideas.explanation: Kelkar's frame, invoked by Ajay: officials want to live tomorrow the way they lived yesterday — they have no incentive to surrender budgets or subordinates to a contracted-out future. Change has to be entrepreneurial, and politicians are the entrepreneurs of public policy. The reform path is to seed ideas in the discourse, get them to bubble up to leadership, and let leadership then push them top-down. Examples include the post-Vajpayee birth of NHAI as a contract-first highway authority — a proof of concept that this kind of structural pivot is possible in India.

core_ideas.concept: Frédéric Bastiat's Seen and Unseen Applied to State Science
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's most pointed counterargument to Ajay's defence of post-1947 science investments. Yes, the IITs and BARC seeded India's IT industry — that is the seen. But what would have happened if the money had stayed with the poor it was coerced from? And what cultural cost did the very technocratic-statist mindset extract by suppressing freedom and society's bottom-up problem-solving for decades? Both are unseen but real. A serious appraisal of state innovation has to count both ledgers.
core_ideas.quote: There was money coerced from the poor of India to set up IITs and all that. We don't see the unseen effect of that.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's reframing of the Indian-vs-foreign R&D question. The classic subsidiarity principle says government action should always be pushed to the lowest viable level — village over state, state over nation. The innovation-policy version is its inverse: in knowledge, push the action to the level that is uniquely capable of producing it. If Nvidia is making the semiconductors, free-ride; if no one else will study Indian mosquitoes or social institutions, do it ourselves. Adoption first, original work for the residual.
core_ideas.quote: What you're saying is that whatever you can take from the world, take it from the world.

core_ideas.concept: Tribal Loyalty as Enemy of Social Science
core_ideas.explanation: A more subtle point Ajay slips in while explaining why the humanities and social sciences cannot be free-ridden. To do good social science about your own country you must first be willing to detach from your tribe — to stop arguing for Gujarat or against Gujarat and just to study India. The deepest obstacle to high-quality Indian social science is therefore not funding but the temptation to advocacy. The state-funded research model has to consciously protect against this.
core_ideas.quote: We need to foster the scientific ability to detach ourselves from our loyalty to India.

core_ideas.explanation: Why governments, structurally, cannot fund risky research. The Indian state operates under audit logic where failure is not a feature of research but a sign of malfeasance — 'you spent the money, you bought the parts, and nothing worked? CBI investigation.' This makes parallel rival pathways impossible: only safe projects pass internal approval, and once a project is chosen its champions politically destroy rivals. Contracting out, by contrast, lets the state legitimately fund six teams, expect five to fail, and not be hauled before auditors for the failures.
core_ideas.quote: The Stalinist idea in government is everything works correctly.

core_ideas.explanation: How the French military funds R&D — including the Rafale fighter — through private corporations like Dassault. The mechanism is the cost-plus contract: the state effectively pays for the risk-taking the private firm absorbs, with explicit upside. The military poses the capability challenge ('I want this set of capabilities at this altitude'); private firms compete on R&D paths to deliver it. India's GFR has no concept of cost-plus or grants — only fixed-price contracts where failure equals breach. Adding these chapters to the GFR is the foundational legal step.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening: 'I am an organic human being. I am flesh and blood. I was born biologically and I will die biologically. Organic matter, it's a great weakness I know, but that's who I am, I accept it. This man, on the other hand, is a bionic man.'
Ajay on his metal implants: 'Sadly no batteries and no CPUs.' And on the airport problem: it goes screaming through security, so 'it's better to wear half-sleeve shirts at airports.'

Ajay on government propaganda being cheaper than space programmes: 'You could just fund a cricket team or something. Or you know, hire a visual effects team and claim that you sent a craft to the moon.'
Amit's catch-line for the NASA section, riffing on Vegas: 'What happens in NASA doesn't stay in NASA.'

Ajay on the Huntsville origin: 'If you get 200 Nazis into a tiny hick town filled with cows and peasants, two generations later it turns into magic.' Amit's deadpan reply: 'I hope it's not leading to a normative place that find 200 Nazis and round them up. Though it won't be as difficult as it seems in the current day.'

Amit on the Mars Orbiter Mission boast: 'They will send a craft to orbit Mars with a claimed total spending that is lower than the cost of that beautiful movie The Martian.' Used to set up the point that hermetic state achievements buy bragging rights but not spillovers.

Ajay's mini pop quiz when it starts raining mid-recording. He names two songs about rain: 'Why Does It Always Rain on Me?' (Travis) and 'I'm Only Happy When It Rains' (Garbage). Amit fails to identify Garbage. Ajay: 'Clearly you're not a nineties kid. This is sad.'

Ajay on what risk-taking looks like in an Indian government setting: 'How will you explain to the CAG — we tried this and it did not work? You paid salaries, you purchased so many parts... how can it be? We should have a CBI investigation.'
Amit on his old day job: 'I used to be a professional limerick writer for The Times of India and I had a limerick on the mosquitoes of Versova.'

Frédéric Bastiat's 'seen and the unseen' — Amit invokes the nineteenth-century French liberal economist's framework to dispute Ajay's IIT-seeded-IT story: the seen benefit is real; the unseen cost (of the coerced money and the technocratic mindset) is also real.

'Every electron is the same and every love is different' — attributed by Ajay to Heisenberg, used to argue that the humanities and social sciences (every love different) cannot be standardised across countries the way physics (every electron the same) can.

Larry Summers's tree: 'If a tree will take twenty years to grow, then I want to run outside and plant the sapling right now.' Used to brush off the objection that the proposed reforms will take decades.
Yashwant Sinha: 'India lives in many different centuries at once' — invoked to defend continued state engagement with frontier science even while medieval India is still being addressed.
'When Ideas Have Sex' — Matt Ridley's famous talk title, used by Amit as a vivid label for what contracting-out R&D physically produces in society.
Suyash Rai's argument against demonetisation — invoked by Amit to make the moral point that aggregate cost-benefit cannot justify a policy when the costs and benefits accrue to different people.
DARPA — held up as the legendary US risk-taking research agency behind TCP/IP and driverless cars; the model for one of the new organisations Ajay's paper proposes for India.

The 1958 Science Policy Resolution — reproduced in Ajay's paper as 'goosebump material,' invoked as the dreamy founding charter of post-independence Indian science whose dream survives even where its method does not.
